title: Convert a stream to a parallel stream and sum all salaries — explain when parallelism helps vs hurts.
shortTitle: Convert a stream to a parallel stream and sum all salaries, explaining when parallelism helps vs hurts

s1_definition.profdef: `stream().parallel()` (or `parallelStream()`) splits work across the common ForkJoinPool. For an associative reduction like summing salaries it can speed up large datasets, but for small data or cheap operations the coordination overhead makes it slower.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya can hire many clerks to each total part of the ledger and then combine their subtotals. That helps when the ledger is huge, but for a short ledger the time spent splitting and coordinating costs more than it saves.
s1_definition.oneliner: Parallel sum helps for large data and expensive work, but hurts for small data due to split/merge overhead.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `stream().parallel()` (or `parallelStream()`) splits work across the common ForkJoinPool. For an associative reduction like summing salaries it can speed up large datasets, but for small data or cheap operations the coordination overhead makes it slower.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Priya can hire many clerks to each total part of the ledger and then combine their subtotals. That helps when the ledger is huge, but for a short ledger the time spent splitting and coordinating costs more than it saves.

**One line to remember:** Parallel sum helps for large data and expensive work, but hurts for small data due to split/merge overhead.

sections.s2_technical:
`list.stream().parallel().mapToDouble(Employee::getSalary).sum()` splits the data into chunks processed on multiple threads from the common ForkJoinPool, then combines the partial sums. Summing is associative, so the parallel result is correct regardless of how the work is split.

Parallelism helps when the dataset is large and the per-element work or the total work is substantial enough to outweigh the fixed cost of splitting, scheduling, and merging. It hurts for small datasets, cheap per-element operations, or data structures that split poorly (like LinkedList), where that fixed overhead dominates and the sequential version is faster.

The senior nuance is that parallel streams share the common ForkJoinPool, so a slow or blocking task can starve other parallel work across the application — I never do blocking I/O in a parallel stream. I only parallelise after measuring, with large n, cheap-to-split sources like arrays or ArrayList, and associative, stateless operations. For money precision I would sum in BigDecimal; parallel double sums can also differ slightly in rounding due to grouping order.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A nightly batch at the National Bank of India sums salaries over millions of records, and the team evaluates whether parallelism actually helps.

This is exactly what a parallel reduction illustrates — it can speed up a huge associative sum but adds overhead that hurts on small inputs.

The code defines a `PayrollSumService with sequential and parallel sums and a demo.
sections.s5_journey:
Input: five employees with salaries 100000 through 100004.

Step 1: The sequential sum walks all five on one thread and totals 500010.

Step 2: The parallel sum splits the five across threads, each computing a partial sum.

Step 3: The partial sums are combined; because addition is associative the total is the same 500010.

Step 4: For this tiny input the parallel version is actually slower due to split and merge overhead, even though the result matches.

```
INFO: sequential sum: 500010.0
INFO: parallel sum  : 500010.0
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  sequential: [E0..E4] → one thread → 500010
  parallel:   [E0..E4] → split → [E0,E1][E2,E3][E4]
                       → partial sums → combine → 500010
     correct (associative) but overhead > benefit for small n
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```
  ═══ HLD — Parallel vs Sequential Salary Sum ═══

  large n + cheap split + associative op → parallel faster
  small n / cheap op / poor-split source → sequential faster
     (parallel uses shared common ForkJoinPool)
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — parallel reduction trade-offs ═══

  ┌─ when parallel helps / hurts ──────────────────────────────┐
  │ parallel().mapToDouble(salary).sum() → split + merge        │
  │ sum is ASSOCIATIVE → correct regardless of split order      │
  │ HELPS: large n, expensive work, splittable source (array)   │
  │ HURTS: small n, cheap op, LinkedList, shared pool contention│
  │ never block in parallel stream (starves common pool)        │
  │ measure first; exact money → BigDecimal                     │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │          PayrollSumService    │
  │  + sumSequential(List): double  │ stream.sum
  │  + sumParallel(List): double     │ parallelStream.sum
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  Call chain:
  1. parallelStream().mapToDouble(salary)
  2. sum() (split → partial sums → combine)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
To sum salaries in parallel I call parallelStream, or parallel on an existing stream, then mapToDouble and sum. The work is split into chunks processed on multiple threads from the common ForkJoinPool, and because addition is associative the partial sums combine into the correct total regardless of how the data was split.

Parallelism helps when the dataset is genuinely large and the work is substantial enough to outweigh the fixed cost of splitting, scheduling, and merging, and when the source splits cheaply, like an array or ArrayList. It hurts for small datasets, cheap per-element operations, or poorly-splitting sources like a LinkedList, where that overhead dominates and the plain sequential stream is faster. At the National Bank of India I would only parallelise a nightly batch over millions of records after measuring that it actually wins.

The senior point I stress is the shared common ForkJoinPool: all parallel streams in the application share it, so a slow or blocking task starves the others, which is why I never do blocking I/O inside a parallel stream. I parallelise only with large n, splittable sources, and associative, stateless operations, and I measure rather than assume. I also note that for exact money I sum in BigDecimal, and that parallel double sums can differ slightly in rounding because the grouping order of additions changes.

---

keyPoints: parallelStream() or stream().parallel() for multi-core processing
Not always faster — overhead for small data, shared mutable state bugs
Use for: large datasets, CPU-bound operations, independent elements
